items.title: The Second Summary Matched Back to the Earlier Teaching

items.zh: 謂如說言：由正思擇食於所食。云何為遠離欲樂行邊受諸飲食？謂如說言：不為倡蕩、不為憍逸、不為飾好、不為端嚴食於所食。云何為遠離自苦行邊受諸飲食？謂如說言：為除飢渴、為斷故受、為令新受當不更生、為當存養若力若樂食於所食。云何為攝受梵行受諸飲食？謂如說言：為攝梵行、為得無罪安隱而住食於所食。
items.en: It is said: through correct discernment in eating what is eaten. …What is it to eat in order to avoid the extreme of indulgence? It is said: not for wanton pleasure, not for pride, not for grooming, not for elegance. …What is it to eat in order to avoid the extreme of self-mortification? It is said: to remove hunger and thirst, to end the old feeling [of illness], to prevent new feeling [of illness] from arising, and to preserve strength and ease. …What is it to eat in order to support pure conduct? It is said: to support pure conduct, and to attain blameless, peaceful abiding.

items.title: A Third Summary: Balanced and Unbalanced Eating

items.zh: 復次，應知此中略義，謂有二種。一、無所食，二、有所食。無所食者，謂一切種都無所食；無所食故，即便夭沒。有所食者，有其二種。一、平等食，二、不平等食。平等食者，謂非極少食、非極多食、非不宜食、非不消食、非染污食。不平等食者，謂或極少食、或極多食、或不宜食、或不消食、或染污食。
items.en: Furthermore, the summary meaning here should be understood as twofold: not eating at all, and eating. Not eating at all means eating nothing whatsoever in any manner; through not eating at all, one simply perishes. Eating is of two kinds: balanced eating and unbalanced eating. Balanced eating means not eating too little, not eating too much, not eating what is unsuitable, not eating before what came before has digested, and not eating in a defiled manner. Unbalanced eating means eating too little, or too much, or unsuitably, or without digestion, or in a defiled manner.

items.zh: 當知此中，由平等食非極少食，令身飢羸未生不生，已生斷滅。由平等食非極多食，身無沈重，有所堪能，堪任修斷。如前廣說。由平等食非不宜食、非不消食，能斷故受，不生新受；由是因緣，當得存養若力若樂。由平等食非染污食，當得無罪安隱而住。由極少食，雖存壽命，而有飢羸，亦少存活。由極多食，如極重擔鎮壓其身，不能以時所食消變。由不消食，或住身中成不消病，或生隨一身諸病苦。如不消食，由不宜食，當知亦爾。此不宜食有差別者，謂於身中集諸過患，由此復觸極重病苦。由染污食，非法追求諸飲食已，有染有愛、耽嗜、饕餮，如前廣說而受用之。由此受用平等所食，及以遠離不平等食，故說於食平等所作。即此於食平等所作，廣以諸句宣示開顯，所謂說言：由正思擇食於所食，不為倡蕩、不為憍逸、不為飾好、不為端嚴，如前廣說。此中說言：由正思擇食於所食，不為倡蕩、不為憍逸、不為飾好、不為端嚴，為身安住、為暫支持。由此遮止都無所食。若復說言：為除飢渴、為攝梵行，廣說乃至安隱而住。由此遮止不平等食。云何遮止不平等食？謂若說言：為除飢渴。由此遮止所食極少。若復說言：為攝梵行。由此遮止所食極多。
items.en: It should be understood here that through balanced eating — not eating too little — hunger and weakness of the body that have not yet arisen do not arise, and those that have arisen are ended. Through balanced eating — not eating too much — the body is not heavy but capable, fit for cultivation and abandonment, as explained at length above. Through balanced eating — not eating what is unsuitable, and not eating before digestion — one is able to end old feeling and keep new feeling from arising; for this reason one will obtain nourishment, strength, and ease. Through balanced eating — not eating in a defiled manner — one will dwell blamelessly and in comfort. Eating too little, though one stays alive, one suffers hunger and weakness and barely survives. Eating too much, the food weighs down the body like an extremely heavy burden, and what is eaten cannot be digested in due time. Eating before digestion, the food either remains in the body as the illness of indigestion, or gives rise to one or another bodily illness and pain. As it is with eating before digestion, so too it should be understood with eating what is unsuitable. What distinguishes eating what is unsuitable is that it accumulates various disorders within the body, and through this one again meets with extremely severe illness and pain. Eating in a defiled manner means that, having sought food and drink contrary to the Dharma, one consumes it with defilement and craving, with indulgence and gluttony, as explained at length above. Because one consumes what is eaten in a balanced way and keeps far from unbalanced eating, it is called acting in balance with regard to food. This acting in balance with regard to food is proclaimed and revealed at length through various phrases, namely, it is said: 'Through correct discernment one eats what is eaten, not for wanton pleasure, not for pride and indulgence, not for grooming, not for elegance,' and so on at length, as above. Here it is said: 'Through correct discernment one eats what is eaten, not for wanton pleasure, not for pride and indulgence, not for grooming, not for elegance, but for the body to abide and to sustain it temporarily.' By this, not eating at all is rejected. It is further said: 'To remove hunger and thirst, to support pure conduct,' and so on at length, down to 'dwelling in comfort'. By this, unbalanced eating is rejected. How is unbalanced eating rejected? When it is said, 'to remove hunger and thirst', by this, eating too little is rejected. When it is further said, 'to support pure conduct', by this, eating too much is rejected.

items.title: Section: Moderation in Eating Closes, and Fascicle 23 Reaches Its End

items.zh: 若復說言：為斷故受、為令新受當不更生。由此遮止不消而食、食所匪宜。若復說言：為當存養、為當得力。由此顯示不極少食、不極多食。若復說言：為當得樂。由此顯示消已而食，及食所宜。若復說言：為當無罪安隱而住。由此顯示無染污食。所以者何？若以非法追求飲食，得已染愛，如前廣說而受用之，名染污食，亦名有罪。若於善品勤修習者，於住空閑瑜伽作意、受持、讀誦、思惟義中，由彼諸惡不善尋思，令心流漏、令心相續，隨順、趣向、臨入而轉，由是因緣，不安隱住。此安隱住復有二種。一者、遠離所食極多，由是因緣，身無沈重，有所堪能，堪任修斷，如前廣說。二者、於食不生味著，由是因緣，遠離諸惡尋思擾動不安隱住。是故如此一切諸句，皆為宣示開顯於食平等所作。如是名為廣略宣說於食知量。
items.en: Furthermore, it is said: to end the old feeling [of illness], and to prevent new feeling [of illness] from arising — by this, eating before digestion and eating what is unsuitable are rejected. It is said: to preserve life, and to attain strength — by this, eating neither too little nor too much is revealed. It is said: to attain ease — by this, eating only after digestion, and eating what is suitable, are revealed. It is said: to attain blameless, peaceful abiding — by this, undefiled eating is revealed. Why is this so? If one seeks food unlawfully and, having obtained it, eats it with attachment and craving as explained at length before, this is called defiled eating, and is also called blameworthy. If one who diligently cultivates wholesome states … through unwholesome deliberation, the mind leaks and continues, following, tending, and turning towards it as one is about to enter concentration — by this cause, one does not abide peacefully. This peaceful abiding is itself twofold: first, avoiding eating too much, by which the body is not heavy and remains capable, fit for cultivation, as explained at length before; second, not developing a taste for food, by which one avoids the disturbance and unrest that unwholesome deliberation about food would otherwise bring. Therefore, all these phrases together are set forth to reveal even application in eating. This is called the broad and brief teaching on moderation in eating.

blocks.text: The last day of fascicle 23: what balanced eating is, and how the whole teaching on food fits together. A long explanatory passage (0411a08–b05) is missing from Ru-Yi's translation; the English column gives our own translation, marked as ours.

"Not for indulgence, pride, grooming, or elegance" avoids the extreme of indulgence. "Removing hunger, healing illness, preventing illness, preserving strength" avoids self-mortification. "Supporting the holy life, blameless peaceful abiding" is the middle. Master Cháng Bǎi: the Buddha taught neither too much pleasure nor too much hardship.
"Balanced eating means not eating too little, not too much, not what is unsuitable, not before the previous meal has digested, and not in a defiled manner."

Not too little: hunger and weakness do not arise. Not too much: the body is not heavy and is fit for practice. Not unsuitable and not undigested: old illness ends and new does not arise, and strength and ease are preserved. Not defiled: one abides blameless and at peace. Too little keeps one alive but weak; too much weighs on the body "like a heavy load"; undigested or unsuitable food causes disease; defiled eating means obtaining food improperly and eating it with craving. The earlier phrases are then matched to these: "for the body's abiding" rules out not eating at all; "to remove hunger" rules out eating too little; "to support the holy life" rules out eating too much.

Two benefits for one about to enter the path: not eating too much, so the body is not heavy; not developing a taste for food, so the mind is not disturbed by thoughts of it. Venerable Miào Jìng: if food has not digested, don't eat; "a little hunger is better".

quiz.q: Which earlier phrases correspond to eating to avoid the extreme of indulgence?
options: not for wanton pleasure, pride, grooming, or elegance
quiz.why: "It is said: not for wanton pleasure, not for pride, not for grooming, not for elegance." Venerable Miào Jìng: wanton pleasure is in fact sexual desire — one does not eat for that.

quiz.q: Which phrases correspond to eating to support pure conduct, and what teaching of the Buddha does Master Cháng Bǎi cite on the two extremes?
options: not for wanton pleasure; the Buddha taught austerity
through correct discernment; the Buddha taught eating more
to support pure conduct and to attain blameless, peaceful abiding; the Buddha said neither too much pleasure nor too much pain
to remove hunger; the Buddha said anything goes
quiz.why: "It is said: to support pure conduct, and to attain blameless, peaceful abiding." Master Cháng Bǎi: the Buddha said one should be neither too pleasure-seeking nor too harsh with oneself.

quiz.q: What five "nots" define balanced eating in the treatise?
options: not vegetarian, meat, cold, hot, or sweet
not too little, not too much, not unsuitable, not before digestion, not defiled
not at any time of day
not cooked, begged, invited, bought, or stolen
quiz.why: "Balanced eating means not eating too little, not eating too much, not eating what is unsuitable, not eating before what came before has digested, and not eating in a defiled manner." Master Cháng Bǎi on undigested eating: watch that what goes in matches what comes out, and don't eat more when food hasn't digested.

quiz.q: What example does Venerable Miào Jìng give of "defiled eating"?
options: strong attachment — eating lots of what one likes and refusing what one doesn't
quiz.why: "Unbalanced eating means eating too little, or too much, or unsuitably, or without digestion, or in a defiled manner." Venerable Miào Jìng: when attachment is strong — eating much of what one likes and refusing what one dislikes — that is all clinging.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what do "healing past illness and preventing new illness" rule out?
options: eating before digestion and eating what is unsuitable
quiz.why: "By this, eating before digestion and eating what is unsuitable are rejected." Venerable Miào Jìng: if food hasn't digested, don't eat — a little hunger is better — and don't eat what is unsuitable.

quiz.q: How does Venerable Miào Jìng explain "about to enter" in "following, tending, and turning towards it as one is about to enter"?
options: while practising yogic attention in solitude and just about to enter the noble path, one turns instead to unwholesome thoughts
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "about to enter" is when, dwelling in solitude and practising yogic attention, one is just on the verge of entering the noble path — and then the mind turns into unwholesome deliberation. The English "about to enter concentration" roughly agrees.

quiz.q: What two kinds of peaceful abiding does the treatise name?
options: avoiding eating too much (body light, fit for cultivation), and not developing a taste for food (free of disturbing thoughts)
quiz.why: First, avoiding eating too much, so the body is not heavy; second, not developing a taste for food, so one avoids the disturbance of unwholesome deliberation. Master Cháng Bǎi: not relishing food means not insisting on having some particular food.
